opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the fastest sustained growth rates of any technology we have good data on. If you look at the period since roughly 2010, when deep learning really took off, the amount of compute used to train the largest models has been growing by something like four to five times per year. To put that in perspective, Moore's law at its peak, the doubling of transistor counts every couple of years, works out to roughly 40 percent growth per year. So we're talking about a rate that's an order of magnitude faster in growth terms than the thing people usually point to as the canonical example of rapid technological progress.

And compounding makes it even more striking. Fourfold per year means about a factor of a million over a decade. If you compare that to things like the scaling of solar photovoltaic deployment, or genome sequencing costs falling, or the spread of mobile phones, those were all remarkably fast, but very few of them sustained this pace for this long. Sequencing costs had a period of very rapid decline, but it was relatively brief by comparison.

It's also worth being clear about what's driving it, because it isn't mostly hardware getting better. Hardware price-performance improves maybe 30 to 40 percent a year. Most of the growth comes from people being willing to spend far more money, building bigger clusters, training for longer, and buying many more chips. So it's largely an investment story: the economic returns, or the perceived returns, have been large enough that labs and their backers keep scaling spending by multiples every year.

That has implications for how long this can continue. You can't increase spending fourfold a year forever. At some point you run into constraints: how much capital people will commit, how many chips fabs can produce, how much power you can bring to a single site, and possibly data. Our work at Epoch has tried to look at these bottlenecks, and our sense is that it's plausible this trend continues through the end of the decade, yielding training runs maybe several thousand times larger than today's frontier. But beyond that, sustaining it would require AI to generate economic value on a scale comparable to a meaningful fraction of the world economy. So historically it's unprecedented, and whether it continues depends on whether AI delivers returns that justify it.

r002.rationale: It calls the pace one of the fastest sustained technology growth rates with good data and compares it with solar deployment, genome sequencing, and mobile phone adoption.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to say is that fourfold per year is just an extraordinary rate. If you compound that out, you get roughly a thousandfold increase every five years, so the models being trained today are using something like a thousand times the compute of the frontier models from around 2019 or 2020. That's not a gradual improvement in a technology, it's more like the entire scale of the enterprise changing every few years.

To put it in historical perspective, the comparison people reach for is Moore's law, and I think that's actually useful because it shows just how unusual this is. Moore's law, the doubling of transistor density roughly every two years, works out to about 1.4x per year. And Moore's law is held up as one of the most remarkable sustained exponential trends in the history of technology. Compute for training AI systems has been growing about three times faster than that on an annual basis, and it's been doing so for over a decade now. So we're seeing something that outpaces what's generally considered the paradigmatic example of rapid technological progress.

The way to understand how that's possible is that the growth is coming from multiple sources stacking on top of each other. Hardware is getting better, so you get the Moore's law component plus specialized architectures for AI workloads. But the much larger driver is simply that people are spending more. Training budgets have grown from something that a few researchers could run on a handful of GPUs to clusters costing hundreds of millions, now heading toward billions of dollars. And then on top of that, training runs have gotten longer. So you're compounding improvements in price-performance with a massive increase in investment with longer run durations, and that's what gets you to fourfold a year.

If you go back further, before around 2010, AI compute grew more or less in line with Moore's law. Researchers mostly used whatever hardware was available, and so the trend just tracked the hardware. What changed in the deep learning era is that compute became the thing people deliberately scaled, because it was clear that scaling it produced better results. So the trend went from being a passive consequence of hardware progress to being an active investment decision, and that's where you see the break to this much steeper trajectory.

The other historical lens I'd offer is economic. When you look at past technological transitions, the build-out of railroads, electrification, the early internet, you see periods where capital investment in a particular technology grows very rapidly for a stretch, often faster than the broader economy for a decade or more. The AI compute build-out has that flavor. The investment is growing much faster than GDP, which means it's taking up a rising share of economic activity. Historically those kinds of trends don't go on forever. They run until they hit some constraint, whether that's financial, or energy, or the supply of chips, or the returns start to diminish. So part of what we try to do is ask how long this particular trend can plausibly continue before it runs into those limits, and our sense is that it can likely be sustained for a number of years yet, but not indefinitely at this pace.

r001.rationale: The response says AI training compute has grown about three times faster than Moore’s law and that this pace has continued for over a decade.

r002.rationale: It describes Moore’s law as one of history’s most remarkable sustained exponential trends, then says AI training compute growth is about three times faster and outpaces that benchmark.

astra-6.text:
A fourfold increase each year is roughly a thousandfold increase over five years, or a millionfold over a decade. So even by the standards of computing, that’s an extraordinarily fast rate of growth.

For comparison, the familiar Moore’s law pace of doubling roughly every two years amounts to about a thirtyfold increase over a decade. Training compute growing fourfold annually is much faster because it isn’t just driven by better chips. You can also use more chips and devote more money to an individual training run.

That distinction matters when we think about how long the trend can continue. Improvements in hardware can sustain growth, but increasing spending at that pace eventually runs into economic constraints. So this is a remarkable period of expansion, but we should be cautious about extrapolating it indefinitely.

sol-6.1.text:
A fourfold increase each year is an extraordinarily fast rate of growth. It means that over five years, the amount of compute used in a training run increases by roughly a thousandfold, and over ten years by about a millionfold.

For comparison, Moore’s law is usually described as a doubling every two years. Fourfold annual growth is two doublings every year, so the doubling time is about six months. That’s much faster than the historical improvement in chips alone.

The distinction is that training compute also grows because developers use more chips and spend more money on individual runs. So this trend reflects both technological progress and an increasing commitment of resources to AI. It’s an exceptional pace, and one that becomes increasingly demanding to sustain.
